meta.title: Oedipus Rex: The Full Story Explained (Sophocles)

scenes.narration: A great king hunts the criminal who cursed his city, not knowing the man he hunts is himself. This is Oedipus Rex.
scenes.notes: Hook before any title. ~26 words, minimal pauses. Names the work.

scenes.narration: Oedipus Rex, by Sophocles, first staged in Athens around four hundred and twenty-nine before Christ.

Three things worth knowing before we begin. First: Oedipus Rex — 'Oedipus the King' — is the most famous tragedy of ancient Greece, written by Sophocles nearly two and a half thousand years ago, and it has been regarded, almost ever since, as the model of what a tragedy should be. The philosopher Aristotle, writing not long after, held it up as the perfect example of the form, and playwrights and thinkers have studied it as a kind of blueprint for tragic drama all the way down to our own day. Second: it draws on a myth every Athenian in the original audience already knew by heart — the dreadful story of Oedipus, the man fated to kill his own father and marry his own mother. And that changes how the play works. The audience knows the horrible truth from the very first line; Oedipus does not. So the entire drama runs on what we call dramatic irony — the unbearable gap between what we know and what the hero, confidently and disastrously, does not. Every proud, determined thing Oedipus says to uncover the truth, we hear double, because we can see the pit he is digging for himself. And third: beneath the horror it is a profound meditation on fate and free will — on whether a man can escape his destiny, and on the terrible knowledge that he cannot; and it is also, astonishingly, the first great detective story, in which the brilliant investigator hunts a murderer through clue after clue, only to discover, at the end of the trail, that the criminal he has sworn to destroy is himself. It all unfolds in a single day, in a single place, before the palace of Thebes — a city in the grip of a deadly plague. A word on the Greek stage it was made for, because it shapes everything. This was religious theatre, performed once, at a great civic festival, before much of the city, with masked actors and a chanting, dancing Chorus of Theban elders who comment on the action and speak, in a sense, for the community and for us. The violence all happens offstage and is reported by messengers — the Greeks found the horror more powerful heard than seen — so the play is built not out of spectacle but out of speech: argument, revelation, and the slow, inexorable extraction of a terrible truth. And it obeys what later critics called the unities: one place, the steps before the palace; one unbroken stretch of time, a single day; one tightening action. Nothing wanders. Everything drives toward the centre. Knowing that, you can feel how the form itself becomes a kind of trap closing — no subplots, no escape, no relief, just one man and the truth moving toward each other across a single afternoon. So let us begin there, at the palace steps, with a king who believes he can save his people, and does not yet know he is their disease.
scenes.notes: Context: the model Greek tragedy (Aristotle's ideal); the audience knows the myth → dramatic irony (we know, Oedipus doesn't); fate vs free will; the first detective story where the investigator IS the criminal; unity of time/place — one day at Thebes in plague.

scenes.narration: A terrible plague has fallen on the city of Thebes. The crops are blighted, the cattle and the people are dying, women miscarry, and a cloud of death hangs over the whole land. A crowd of desperate suppliants gathers at the palace steps to beg help from their king — and what a king he is. Oedipus is the most admired man in Thebes, beloved and revered, because years before he saved the city from a monster: the Sphinx, a riddling creature that had strangled every traveller who failed to answer her question, until Oedipus alone solved her riddle and freed Thebes from her terror. In gratitude the city made him king, and gave him the hand of its recently widowed queen, Jocasta — for Thebes had just lost its former king, Laius, murdered on a journey, no one knew by whom. The whole arrangement seemed, at the time, like the just reward of a saviour: the brilliant young outsider who freed the city crowned as its ruler and married to its queen. No one paused to wonder at the dark coincidences folded into that happy ending — that the king had died just before the stranger arrived, that the stranger was exactly old enough, that the riddle-solver who could answer the Sphinx had never been able to answer the simplest question of all, the question of where he himself came from. The city's gratitude and Oedipus's own glory buried all of it. For years Thebes prospered under him and he reigned in honour, the model of a successful king, with Jocasta at his side and children growing in the palace. And then the plague came, and with it the slow turning-over of that buried ground. Now, as the plague rages, the people turn again to this clever, decisive, caring ruler to save them a second time. Oedipus, every inch the responsible king, has already acted: he has sent his brother-in-law Creon to consult the great oracle of Apollo at Delphi, to ask how the plague can be lifted. Creon returns with the god's answer, and it is a grim one. Thebes harbours a pollution, a hidden crime that must be driven out: the murderer of the former king, Laius, who was killed years ago and whose death was never avenged, is living unpunished within the city. Find the killer of Laius, says the oracle, and banish or execute him, and the plague will lift. And Oedipus, with absolute confidence, throws the whole force of his will and his intelligence into the hunt, vowing publicly to track down the unknown murderer and rid the city of him, whoever he may prove to be. It is worth pausing on how admirable Oedipus is in this opening — because the tragedy depends on it. He is no tyrant; he is a genuinely good king, quick, caring, decisive, who feels his people's suffering as his own and has already acted to relieve it before they even ask. The very qualities that make him great — his restless intelligence, his refusal to leave a riddle unsolved, his fierce determination to protect his city and face the truth head-on — are precisely the qualities that will destroy him. This is the heart of Greek tragedy: the hero is brought down not by a vice but, in a terrible sense, by his virtues pushed to their limit, by being exactly the man he is. Oedipus hunts the truth because he is the kind of man who must; and the truth, when he finds it, annihilates him. The audience, knowing what he does not, watches this good king stride so boldly toward the edge of the cliff.
scenes.notes: Plague on Thebes; Oedipus the revered king who once saved the city by solving the Sphinx's riddle (and won the widowed queen Jocasta); he sent Creon to the Delphic oracle; the answer — Thebes harbours Laius's unpunished murderer; find & expel him to lift the plague; Oedipus vows to hunt the killer.

scenes.narration: Here Sophocles springs the first and greatest of the play's terrible ironies. Oedipus, determined to flush out the hidden killer, makes a grand public proclamation: he solemnly curses the unknown murderer of Laius, and anyone who shelters him. Let the murderer's life be wretched; let him be driven out, friendless and accursed, from every home and every altar. And Oedipus goes further still — he declares that if the killer should prove to be living secretly under his own roof, then may the curse fall upon himself as well. He means it as a show of his own righteousness and resolve; he has no idea that he is standing in the marketplace solemnly calling down ruin upon his own head. Every word of the curse will come true, and every word of it he has aimed, unknowing, at himself. The audience, who knows exactly who killed Laius, listens to this proud, sincere, self-damning speech with a kind of horror — and this is the engine that will drive the entire play. Oedipus, the great solver of riddles, the saviour of the city, launches a relentless investigation into a murder, utterly certain that he is the hunter and some other man the prey, and summons, as his first witness, the one person in Thebes said to see what others cannot: the old blind prophet, Tiresias. It is worth noticing just how total the irony of this curse is, because Sophocles layers it several deep. Oedipus promises to fight for the dead king Laius as though for his own father — and Laius was his father. He vows to hunt the killer as if the dead man's own son were doing it — and the killer is that son. He swears the murderer will live out a wretched, blinded, exiled existence — which is precisely the fate he is about to bring down on himself. He even says that the killer, whoever he is, might be living in his own house with his own family — and the killer is the head of that house. Every clause is a prophecy of his own doom, delivered in ringing tones of royal justice by a man who thinks he is talking about someone else entirely. No other play has ever packed so much dramatic irony into a single speech; it is the hinge on which the whole tragedy swings.
scenes.notes: Oedipus publicly curses the unknown murderer (and any who shelter him) — and extends the curse to himself if the killer is under his own roof; crushing dramatic irony (he curses himself); launches the investigation; summons the blind prophet Tiresias.

scenes.narration: Oedipus curses the killer he is hunting — not knowing he is cursing himself.

on_screen.quote: And on the murderer this curse I lay: Wretch, may he pine in utter wretchedness!

scenes.narration: The blind seer can see the whole truth — and the one thing he says, the king cannot bear to hear.

Tiresias is led in — old, blind, and reluctant. Oedipus, courteous at first, asks the famous seer to use his powers and name the murderer. But Tiresias, who can see with his inner sight exactly what the king is and what he has done, recoils in anguish and refuses to speak. He begs to be sent home; he says that knowing the truth is a terrible burden and that it would be better for everyone if he said nothing. His stubborn silence baffles and then enrages Oedipus, whose temper — his great tragic flaw of pride and hot-blooded impatience — now begins to show. The king insults the old man, accuses him of complicity in the murder, even taunts him that for all his gifts of prophecy he is nothing but a useless, scheming fraud. And Tiresias, finally goaded past endurance, speaks. He tells Oedipus the plain, impossible truth: that Oedipus himself is the polluted thing he is hunting; that Oedipus is the murderer of Laius; that the king is living in unspeakable shame with those closest to him and does not know it. He goes further, hinting darkly that the man Oedipus seeks is here, thought a foreigner but truly Theban-born; that he will be revealed as brother and father to his own children, son and husband to the woman who bore him; and that he who now sees clearly will end in blindness, and he who is rich will end a beggar, tapping his way into exile over foreign soil. It is the whole plot, spoken aloud, in the first third of the play — and it glances off Oedipus completely, because he cannot and will not believe a word of it. This is the strange genius of the design: Sophocles tells us everything, early and plainly, through the prophet, and the suspense comes not from wondering what the truth is but from watching the one man who needs to hear it refuse, with all his considerable strength, to let it in. Oedipus cannot, will not, hear it. In his fury he decides the prophet must be lying, part of a plot — and, before the old man is led away, Tiresias, with the authority of the blind who truly see, flings the play's central image back in his face.
scenes.notes: Tiresias led in, reluctant, refuses to name the killer (knowing the burden); Oedipus's pride/temper flares, insults & accuses him; goaded, Tiresias declares Oedipus himself is the murderer & polluted; Oedipus won't believe it; the sight/blindness image.

scenes.narration: The blind prophet to the seeing king — the play's central, devastating image.

on_screen.quote: Thou hast eyes, yet see'st not in what misery thou art fallen, nor where thou dwellest nor with whom for mate.

scenes.narration: The irony here is almost too sharp to bear. Tiresias is physically blind but sees the truth perfectly; Oedipus has his eyes but is utterly blind to who and what he is — and by the end of the play that image will become horrifyingly literal. For now, though, Oedipus hears the prophet's accusation only as an outrage and an attack. He leaps to the conclusion that it is all a conspiracy: that his trusted brother-in-law Creon, hungry for the throne, has bribed Tiresias to brand the king a murderer and drive him out. When Creon appears, protesting his innocence and reasonably pointing out that he already enjoys all the privileges of power without its burdens and has no motive to want the crown, Oedipus will not listen; in his rising paranoia and wounded pride he rages at Creon and threatens him with death. It takes the intervention of the queen, Jocasta, hurrying out of the palace to quell the ugly quarrel between her husband and her brother, to calm the king down. And it is Jocasta, trying in all innocence to soothe Oedipus and to prove to him that prophets and oracles are not to be feared, who will, with a few comforting words, unknowingly light the fuse that blows the whole terrible truth into the open.
scenes.notes: The sight/blindness irony (blind seer sees, sighted king is blind — soon literal); Oedipus suspects a Creon–Tiresias plot for the throne; rages at the innocent Creon, threatens death; Jocasta intervenes to calm them — and will unknowingly trigger the revelation.

scenes.narration: The queen tries to prove oracles are nothing to fear — and says the one word that unlocks the horror.

To comfort her agitated husband, Jocasta tells him not to put any faith in prophets, and offers what she thinks is proof that their predictions are worthless. Long ago, she says, an oracle warned her first husband, King Laius, that he was fated to be killed by his own son. And yet it did not happen, she assures Oedipus — for their infant son was taken away and left to die on a lonely mountainside while still a baby, his little feet pinned together, and Laius was in fact killed years later by a band of robbers, at a place where three roads meet, far from Thebes. So you see, she says triumphantly, the dreadful prophecy came to nothing; no son killed Laius; prophets know nothing. But Oedipus has gone very still. One detail has reached into his chest like a cold hand. A place where three roads meet. He asks her, urgently now, to describe it — when it happened, what Laius looked like, how many were in his party. And as she answers, an old, buried memory rises in Oedipus with mounting dread. For years ago, as a young man, travelling alone, far from home, at a place where three roads met, Oedipus himself quarrelled with an arrogant old stranger and his servants who tried to force him off the path — and in his anger he killed them. The thing he has been hunting all day begins, horribly, to turn and look back at him. Watch how Sophocles works here: it is not the prophet's direct accusation that cracks Oedipus — pride can wave that away as a plot — but a small, stray, factual detail, dropped by his own wife while she is trying to reassure him. A place where three roads meet. It is the investigator's own method turned against him: a clue, an inconsistency, a fact that will not fit, snagging in the mind of a man who cannot leave a puzzle alone. And this is the exquisite cruelty of the structure — that Oedipus will be destroyed not by his enemies but by his virtues, not by the lie of a conspiracy but by his own relentless devotion to the truth. Every instinct that made him a great king and the solver of the Sphinx now bends itself, unstoppably, to the task of proving his own guilt. He could still stop. Jocasta will soon beg him to stop. He cannot. He has to know.
scenes.notes: Jocasta, to calm him, says oracles are worthless: Laius was prophesied to die by his own son, but their baby was exposed to die (feet pinned) and Laius was killed by robbers at a place where three roads meet; the 'three roads' detail terrifies Oedipus — he recalls killing an old man at a crossroads; the dread begins.

scenes.narration: Shaken, Oedipus tells Jocasta his own story for the first time, and the two halves of the puzzle begin to move toward each other. He was raised, he says, as the son of the king and queen of Corinth, a prince with every expectation of happiness — until, at a feast, a drunk man taunted him that he was not truly his father's son. Troubled, Oedipus went secretly to the oracle at Delphi to learn the truth of his birth — and the oracle did not answer that question, but instead told him something monstrous: that he was fated to kill his own father and to marry his own mother. Horrified, loving the parents he believed were his, Oedipus did the only thing he could think of to outrun the prophecy: he fled Corinth and vowed never to return, to keep himself far from the father and mother he meant to protect. And on that flight, on a lonely road, at a place where three roads met, he had been forced into a violent quarrel with an old man in a chariot and his attendants. The old man had struck him in arrogance as the roads met; Oedipus, hot-tempered, had struck back and, in the brawl that followed, killed the old man and, he believed, all but one of his party. He had thought nothing more of it for years — a traveller's deadly roadside quarrel, soon left behind on the way to a new life and a crown. It is a chilling detail of character: the same quick, proud temper that flared just now at Tiresias and at Creon is the temper that, years ago at the crossroads, made Oedipus kill. The flaw was always in him, long before this day; the day only reveals what it has already done. And now, telling the old story to his wife, he hears it for the first time as something other than a closed and forgotten episode. Now, telling it aloud, he is gripped by a terrible fear — that the stranger he killed at the crossroads may have been Laius himself; that he, Oedipus, may be the very murderer he has sworn to hunt and curse and drive from the city. There is one hope left: Jocasta said robbers, plural, killed Laius, and Oedipus was one man. A single surviving witness — an old shepherd, the one member of Laius's party who escaped the slaughter at the crossroads and fled home — could settle it. If he still says robbers, many men, killed the king, then Oedipus is cleared, for he was one man alone. On that one word, plural or singular, Oedipus now pins all his hope. He sends for the shepherd urgently. It is a desperate, narrowing hope, and the audience knows it is false — but notice how even now Oedipus frames the question to save himself, clinging to a discrepancy in the testimony rather than facing the mountain of evidence already before him. This is how the mind protects itself from an unbearable truth: not by ignoring it, but by fixing on one small loophole and pouring all its hope through that. Jocasta, watching her husband, is beginning to go quiet in a different way — and the dread in the royal house thickens as everyone waits for one old man to be brought down from the hills.
scenes.notes: Oedipus's story: raised a prince of Corinth; a drunk's taunt; the Delphic oracle — fated to kill his father & marry his mother; he fled Corinth to escape it; killed an old man & his party at a crossroads; now fears that man was Laius & that he is the killer he hunts; one hope — the surviving shepherd/witness, sent for.

scenes.narration: A messenger arrives with good news from Corinth — and the good news is the worst thing of all.

Now Sophocles tightens the screw with a masterstroke of tragic plotting. A messenger arrives from Corinth with what seems like wonderful news: the old king of Corinth, Polybus — the man Oedipus believes is his father — has died, peacefully, of old age. For a moment there is relief, even joy. Jocasta seizes on it as final proof that oracles are empty: Oedipus's father has died naturally, so the prophecy that Oedipus would kill him is now impossible, broken forever. Oedipus, too, is comforted — yet one fear still gnaws: his mother, the queen of Corinth, is still alive, and the prophecy said he would marry her, so he still dares not go home. And here the messenger, meaning only to be kind, to free the king of his last worry, delivers the blow that destroys him. Do not fear returning to Corinth, he says cheerfully, for the king and queen there were not your real parents at all. And how do I know? Because it was I, years ago, who gave you to them — a tiny baby, received as a gift up on Mount Cithaeron, your little feet pinned and swollen — I who handed you over to be raised as their son. Oedipus, reeling, demands to know where the messenger got the baby. From another shepherd, comes the answer, a servant of the household of King Laius of Thebes. It is the same shepherd Oedipus has already sent for. The two halves of the trap are about to close. This is one of the most admired turns in all of drama, because of its sheer tragic irony: the messenger has travelled a long way bearing what he is sure is happy news, and he delivers each revelation beaming, expecting thanks and reward, cheerfully lifting what he thinks is a weight from the king's mind — and every kindly sentence drives the knife deeper. He means to free Oedipus from the fear of the prophecy; instead he proves it. He means to reassure him he can safely go home; instead he destroys the last wall between Oedipus and the truth. The good news and the catastrophe are the very same words. Sophocles lets us watch the king's face as relief curdles into dawning horror, as the thing he was running from all his life turns out to have been standing beside him, wearing a smile, the whole time.
scenes.notes: Corinthian messenger: King Polybus ('father') has died of old age — Jocasta says the prophecy is void; but Oedipus still fears his 'mother'; the messenger reveals Oedipus was adopted — he himself received the pin-footed baby on Mt Cithaeron & gave him to Corinth; he got the baby from a shepherd of Laius's house — the same shepherd already summoned.

scenes.narration: And now Jocasta understands. Faster than her husband, with a mother's and a wife's dawning horror, she puts the pieces together — the exposed baby with the pinned feet, the son fated to kill his father, the stranger who came from Corinth and solved the Sphinx and married her, the age, the scars, the crossroads — and she realises, all at once, the full and unspeakable truth: that her husband Oedipus is her own son; that the baby she and Laius gave to be killed did not die; that she has married him and borne his children. She turns white, and begs Oedipus, desperately, to stop the investigation, to ask no more questions, to let the matter drop for the love of the gods. But Oedipus, still one fatal step behind her, misreads her terror entirely — he thinks the proud queen is suddenly afraid that the inquiry will reveal him to be of low or shameful birth, a foundling, beneath her. And in a line of piercing, awful irony, he declares that he does not care; that he will know the truth of his birth whatever it is, however humble, because he is a man who must know. Jocasta, seeing he will not be stopped, cries out one last anguished warning — that he is doomed, that she can say no more — and rushes from the stage into the palace. It is the last time Oedipus will see her alive. Jocasta's silence here is one of the great wordless moments in theatre. She has spent the play as the voice of comfort and common sense, waving away oracles, urging her husband not to fear — and now, in a few seconds, she understands that every reassurance she gave was built on the most monstrous truth imaginable, and that she herself is at the centre of it, wife and mother to the same man. Her abrupt, agonised exit says everything her words cannot. And there is a terrible poignancy in the gap between them at this instant: she knows, and is already moving toward death; he does not yet know, and is still eagerly, almost cheerfully, pressing on toward the discovery, misreading her devastation as mere pride. Two people on the same stage, married, bound, and for this one unbearable moment separated by a chasm of knowledge — she seeing the whole abyss, he still hunting the clue that will show it to him. Then she is gone, and he turns, impatient, to the one witness who can finish the story.
scenes.notes: Jocasta works it out first (exposed baby, the prophecy, the stranger she married) — realises Oedipus is her son; begs him to stop the inquiry; he misreads her fear as snobbery about his low birth, vows to know the truth regardless; Jocasta cries a last warning and rushes inside — the last time he sees her alive.

scenes.narration: The last witness is dragged in — and the man who could solve any riddle finally solves the one he should have feared.

The old shepherd is brought in at last — and he, like Tiresias, like Jocasta, does not want to speak; he knows what the truth will do. There is a grim pattern here that the play has traced from the start: everyone who knows the truth tries to stop Oedipus from reaching it. Tiresias begged to be sent home unquestioned. Jocasta begged him to abandon the inquiry. Now the shepherd begs not to be made to answer. The truth in this play is not hidden by a villain; it is guarded by love and pity, by people trying to spare Oedipus a knowledge they can see will destroy him. And against all of them stands Oedipus's own furious will to know, overriding every warning, every plea, every instinct of mercy — including, fatally, the shepherd's. The Corinthian messenger, still cheerfully helpful, recognises the old shepherd as the very man who long ago handed him the baby, and says so; and that recognition between the two herdsmen, the one who received the child and the one who gave it away, snaps the last lock. But Oedipus, now in a fever of determination, threatens him with torture and death until the terrified old man gives up the secret piece by dreadful piece. Yes — long ago he was given a newborn baby to destroy, from the house of Laius. Yes — the child was said to be Laius and Jocasta's own son. Yes — there was a prophecy that the boy would kill his father, and that is why they meant to leave him to die on the mountain, his feet pierced and bound. And no — he did not kill the baby; out of pity he gave it instead to a Corinthian shepherd, to be raised far away. The baby was Oedipus. And so, in a single unbearable moment, the whole truth crashes down on Oedipus entire: that Laius, the man he killed at the crossroads, was his father; that Jocasta, the wife he loves and with whom he has had children, is his mother; that he is the thing the oracle foretold, the pollution poisoning Thebes, the murderer he swore to hunt and the accursed wretch he swore to cast out. Every road he took to escape his fate led him straight into it. The great solver of riddles has solved the final riddle, and the answer is himself. There is a dreadful symmetry the Greeks would have savoured: the Sphinx's riddle, long ago, was 'what goes on four legs, then two, then three?' — and the answer was Man, the creature who crawls as a baby, walks upright in his prime, and leans on a stick in old age. Oedipus answered it brilliantly and won a kingdom. But he never truly knew the deepest form of that riddle — the mystery of a single particular man, his own origin, his own nature, his own name — and that is the riddle that destroys him. He could read all of mankind in the abstract and could not read himself. His very name, it turns out, carries the secret he never decoded: Oedipus means 'swollen foot', the mark of the pinned-together ankles of the baby left to die, the clue he carried in his own flesh his whole life without reading it. With a cry of absolute horror, the answer finally and fully his, he rushes into the palace.
scenes.notes: The shepherd, under threat, confesses piece by piece: given a baby from Laius's house to kill (Laius & Jocasta's son, prophesied to kill his father, feet pierced), spared it out of pity, gave it to the Corinthian — the baby was Oedipus; the whole truth crashes down (killed his father, married his mother, is the pollution he hunted); he rushes inside.

scenes.narration: What happens next is reported, in the Greek way, by a messenger who comes out from the palace, because the Greeks did not show such horrors on stage — but the telling is more terrible than any spectacle. Inside, Oedipus found Jocasta already dead: his wife and mother, unable to live with the truth, had hanged herself in their bedchamber. And Oedipus, howling, cut her down, and took the long golden pins from her gown, and with them struck out his own eyes — again and again — blinding himself, so that he would never have to look upon the father he killed, the mother he married, the children who are also his brothers and sisters, the ruin he had made and could not bear to see. The man who had eyes but was blind to the truth now, knowing the truth at last, puts out his eyes forever: the play's great image made flesh. He staggers out, blood streaming down his face, a broken thing, and begs to be cast out of Thebes — to be sent into exile, as he himself decreed for the murderer, so that the plague will lift and the city be saved. Creon, the man Oedipus had so lately accused of treason and threatened with death, now master of Thebes, treats the fallen king with a cold, correct mercy — a last quiet irony, that the ruined Oedipus must beg favours of the very kinsman he wronged, and receive them not as a king but as a broken suppliant. He who began the day commanding everyone now can command nothing, not even the terms of his own exile. And in the play's most heartbreaking moment, the blind Oedipus asks only to touch and hold his two little daughters, Antigone and Ismene, one last time, grieving for the shamed and ruined life his crime has condemned them to — for who, he asks, will ever marry the daughters of such a father? — before he is led away. There is a question worth sitting with in the blinding, because it is deliberate and strange: why does Oedipus not simply kill himself, as Jocasta did? His own answer, choked out through the blood, is that he could not bear to go down among the dead and face his father and mother with seeing eyes, nor to look ever again on the city, the children, the daylight that his crime has poisoned. Blindness is not an escape but a punishment he chooses and inflicts on himself — a living darkness, so that he must go on existing, exiled and sightless, carrying the full weight of what he is. It is also the play's governing image completed: the man who all along 'had eyes and saw nothing', who was blind to himself while mocking a blind man's sight, now makes his inner blindness visible and permanent. He wanted, above all else, to see the truth; and the truth, once seen, was the one thing he could not go on looking at.
scenes.notes: Reported (offstage): Jocasta has hanged herself; Oedipus cuts her down, takes the gold pins from her gown and blinds himself (so he need not see what he's done) — the sight/blindness image made literal; staggers out bloodied, begs for exile to lift the plague; Creon takes power; Oedipus holds his daughters in farewell; led away.

scenes.narration: The chorus's final warning — the most famous lines in Greek tragedy.

on_screen.quote: Therefore wait to see life's ending ere thou count one mortal blest; wait till free from pain and sorrow he has gained his final rest.

scenes.narration: Why has this one grim day in ancient Thebes gripped audiences for two and a half thousand years? Partly for the sheer, merciless perfection of its construction. The play is a single tightening coil: it begins at the very end of the story, with the crime long past and the plague already raging, and consists of nothing but Oedipus relentlessly uncovering what has already happened — so that the whole drama is one long, dreadful act of discovery, each revelation locking into the last with the precision of a trap, until the hero and the audience arrive together at the horror we saw coming from the first line. It is, structurally, as tight and inevitable as anything ever written for the stage — which is exactly why Aristotle held it up as the model of tragedy, praising its single unbroken action, its reversal and recognition landing together in one stroke, and the way it arouses pity and fear and then purges them. The 'reversal' here is perfect of its kind: the Corinthian messenger arrives to bring Oedipus joy and comfort and, by the very same news, brings him ruin — the single most admired turning-point in Greek drama, where the action pivots on its heel and good news becomes catastrophe in one breath. And the 'recognition' — the moment the hero sees the truth — is not some external token but the discovery of his own identity, which is why it strikes so deep. Oedipus does not merely find out who killed Laius; he finds out who he is. The mystery and the man are the same. But its deeper hold is on the questions it refuses to answer comfortably. It is the great drama of fate and free will: Oedipus does everything a good and clever man could do to escape his destiny — he flees his home, he governs wisely, he hunts the truth courageously — and every single choice drives him faster toward the doom he is fleeing. Is he guilty, when he never knew what he was doing? He did not know the old man at the crossroads was his father, nor the queen his mother; by intention he committed no sin at all. And yet the pollution is real, the plague is real, the horror is real, and Oedipus does not excuse himself by pleading ignorance — he takes the full weight of what he has done upon himself, and punishes himself more terribly than any judge would dare. Is he being punished, then, or simply crushed by a fate assigned before his birth, guilty of nothing but of being the man the gods had marked? Sophocles does not let us off the hook, and that unresolved tension is a large part of the play's enduring power: it refuses to tell us whether Oedipus is a sinner getting his desert or an innocent broken on the wheel of destiny, and holds both before us at once, unbearably. Perhaps the deepest and most frightening suggestion of the play is that it does not finally matter which — that a human life can be destroyed utterly through no clear fault of its own, and that the universe offers no explanation and no appeal. And the play's final wisdom, spoken by the chorus as the blind king is led away, is as bleak and as bracing as anything in literature: that no human being, however powerful, however admired, however clever, can count himself truly fortunate while he still lives, because no one knows what the gods and the next turn of the road may hold — and that the mightiest man in the city can be brought, between dawn and dusk of a single day, lower than the lowest beggar. It is the oldest and hardest lesson, and Sophocles delivers it with a force that has never dimmed. The play has also, of course, given its name to one of the most famous ideas of the modern age: Sigmund Freud took from it his 'Oedipus complex', his theory that the buried wish to possess one parent and displace the other lurks in us all, and chose this ancient story as its emblem — a sign of how deep into the human psyche the play seems to reach, far beyond its own place and time. Whether or not one believes a word of Freud, the instinct behind the choice is sound: that Oedipus's horror is not some freakish curse that could only befall one mythical king, but a kind of distilled nightmare of things half-feared in every family and every self — of hidden origins, of unbearable truths about who we are, of the past we cannot outrun. That is why a play about a Bronze-Age king and a plague can still make a modern audience sit forward in dread. Read it, or see it played — and feel how little stands between any of us and the turning of the wheel.
scenes.notes: Close: why it endures — the merciless construction (starts at the end, all discovery, a tightening trap, Aristotle's model); fate vs free will (every escape drives him toward doom); the guilt question (knew nothing); the chorus's bleak final wisdom — count no one fortunate till death; the mightiest can fall in a single day.

scenes.narration: That's Oedipus Rex — a king who solved every riddle but his own, and uncovered, in a single day, that he was the monster he hunted. If you want more, there are full retellings of the other great books waiting on the channel, with more arriving all the time. It is two and a half thousand years old and still the most perfectly built tragedy ever written — read it, and brace yourself. Thanks for watching.
